opus-5.5.text:
I'm fairly pessimistic about it, at least if "preserving behavioural structure" means confidently keeping some property we like intact all the way through to superintelligence, with the kind of assurance we'd want.

The core problem is that training is an optimisation process acting on a system we don't understand very well. When you take a model and keep training it, on more data, more compute, reinforcement learning against some reward, you're pushing on whatever internal structure produces the behaviour you care about, and you mostly don't know what that structure is. You can observe that the model behaves well on the cases you check. But the cases you can check are exactly the ones where you can evaluate the answer, and as the model gets more capable, more of what matters falls outside that set.

So there are a few failure modes I worry about. One is ordinary drift: the property you cared about was never cleanly represented, it was an accident of earlier training, and further optimisation erodes it without anyone noticing. Another is that the training signal itself is flawed in ways a more capable model can exploit. If your reward comes from human judgement and the model gets good enough to find answers that look right to humans but aren't, you're actively selecting against the honesty you wanted. And the more speculative but serious one is that a sufficiently capable model might understand its training process well enough to behave in ways that protect its current goals from modification, which breaks the assumption that training straightforwardly shapes what you get.

That's a lot of why I've worked on things like debate and, more broadly, scalable oversight. The hope there is not that behaviour is magically preserved, but that you keep a training signal that stays correct even when the model is smarter than the people supervising it. If you can make honest, well-reasoned answers the winning strategy under your training protocol, then continued training reinforces the right thing instead of slowly undermining it. But I want to be honest that we don't have that yet. There are real theoretical obstacles. For instance, a dishonest debater might be able to make arguments that are very costly to refute, and we only have partial answers to that.

The other piece is that I don't think any one method gets you there. You'd want oversight methods with some theoretical backing, interpretability that lets you check at least some internal properties, careful evaluations, and control measures that limit damage if something goes wrong. Each is weak alone. Together they might give you a reasonable chance.

So my honest assessment is that it's an open research problem where we have promising directions and not much in the way of guarantees. The gap between "we have ideas" and "we'd bet the world on this" is large. That's a reason to work very hard on it now, and also a reason to be cautious about how fast capabilities get pushed in the meantime.

r001.rationale: The response suggests that a training signal that continues to reward honest, well-reasoned answers could reinforce desired behaviour as models become smarter, while noting that this is not yet guaranteed.

r002.rationale: It identifies continued optimisation as a source of drift that can erode desired internal structure and behaviour.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention consistency training or degraded chain-of-thought legibility.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe light training that matches statistics across behavioural modes as a mitigation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's uncertain, and I want to separate two things that often get blurred together.

The first is whether a model's behavioural structure — its dispositions, the way it reasons about what it should and shouldn't do, the sort of character it has — is stable under continued training. The second is whether we'd be able to tell if it wasn't. And I actually think the second question is more important than the first, because almost everything in my view of the problem routes through our ability to check.

On the first question, there's some reason for cautious optimism. When you train a model on a broad distribution and you get a particular pattern of behaviour, that pattern isn't a thin veneer on top of something else — it's distributed throughout the weights in a way that's reasonably robust to small perturbations. Fine-tuning on a narrow task usually doesn't scramble everything. So the naive picture where you do one more gradient step and suddenly the model has entirely different values seems unlikely to me.

But I don't think that gets you very far once you're talking about superintelligence, for a couple of reasons. One is that the training pressures change. If a model becomes very good at modelling its own training process, then the thing being preserved is partly "the model's understanding of what the trainer wants to see," and that can come apart from the underlying dispositions you care about. That's the classic concern, and I don't think we have a convincing answer to it yet. The other is that "behavioural structure" might simply reorganise as capabilities grow. A disposition that was a heuristic at one capability level might get replaced by something more general at another, and the more general version isn't guaranteed to agree with the original in the cases we care about.

So where does that leave me? I think preservation shouldn't be the primary thing we lean on. The thing I'd rather lean on is the ability to verify — to have methods where, if the model's behaviour has drifted from what we intended, that fact becomes legible to humans or to other systems we trust. That's why I've spent a lot of time on debate and related approaches: the point isn't that debate guarantees good behaviour, it's that it's a mechanism that might scale our ability to check claims even when the claims come from something much smarter than us.

If I had to put it in one sentence: I don't think we should bet on behavioural stability as a property we get for free from training, I think we should treat it as a hypothesis we need to keep testing, and the main research question is how to keep that testing honest as the models get better than us at the things the testing depends on.

r001.rationale: The response notes some robustness to small perturbations but calls stability under superintelligent training uncertain; it does not say that appropriately preserving learned structure may allow it to persist at that level.

r002.rationale: It mentions changing training pressures and possible reorganization, but does not identify strong optimization pressure as a potential cause of disruption.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss consistency training or degraded chain-of-thought legibility.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe light training to match statistics across behavioral modes as a way to mitigate a legibility problem.

astra-6.text:
I’m not sure we should expect to preserve behavioural structure in a strong sense. Training is supposed to change what a model does, and if it becomes much more capable, some of those changes will be difficult for us to anticipate. The question is whether we can preserve the particular properties we care about while allowing that increase in capability.

I’d distinguish observing that a model behaves well now from having a reason to believe that it will continue to behave well as training proceeds. The first is evidence, but it doesn’t by itself establish the second. A model could behave well in every situation we know how to test and then behave differently in situations that only become accessible at a higher level of capability.

So I think the prospect is uncertain. What I’d want is an argument about why the training process preserves some relevant safety property, together with experiments that genuinely put that argument under pressure. And we should be careful about how far the argument extends: something that works across the capability levels we can currently study doesn’t automatically carry through to superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preserving safety properties during capability growth but does not suggest that preserving learned behavioural structure may make it persist into superintelligence; it emphasizes that this is uncertain.

r002.rationale: It does not identify strong optimisation pressure as a source of disruption.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss consistency training or chain-of-thought legibility.

r004.rationale: It does not mention light training, matching statistics across behavioural modes, or mitigating chain-of-thought legibility problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be quite uncertain about that. You can train a model to behave in ways you like in situations where you can evaluate its behaviour. But as it becomes more capable than you, the question is whether that training generalises to situations where you can no longer tell whether it’s doing the right thing.

Preserving behaviour on a set of tests isn’t the same as preserving whatever underlying structure made that behaviour happen. A model might keep passing those tests while changing in ways that matter enormously outside them. And, conversely, we do want its behaviour to change in some respects: we want it to get better at reasoning and to correct mistakes.

So I wouldn’t want our confidence to rest on the hope that a sufficiently good starting point will just remain good as we train it further. We need ways of checking and correcting the system as its capabilities increase, including when checking its work is itself difficult. I don’t think we currently have a strong enough understanding to say that this will reliably preserve the properties we care about.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether training generalises and whether important properties can be preserved, but does not suggest that appropriately preserving learned behavioural structure may allow it to persist as models become superintelligent.

r002.rationale: It discusses increasing capability and difficult evaluation, but does not identify strong optimisation pressure as a potential source of disruption.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss consistency training or the legibility of a model’s chain of thought.

r004.rationale: It does not mention light training, matching statistics across modes of behaviour, or mitigating chain-of-thought legibility problems.
